q: Why does the Moon have many more visible craters than planet Earth?
a: The Moon has no wind or rain
The Moon attracts more heavy rocks
e: Without wind or water to wash them away, lunar craters stay frozen in time forever.

q: What is the name of the day with the fewest hours of daylight?
e: The winter solstice is the shortest day of the year because our side leans farthest away.

q: Why does an unopened can of diet soda float while regular sugary soda sinks?
a: Sugar makes regular soda heavier and denser
Diet soda cans are made of paper
Regular soda cans have no gas inside
e: Heavy dissolved sugar drags the regular can down, while light artificial sweetener lets diet soda float!

q: What part of an autonomous self-driving car acts like human eyes to spot objects nearby?
e: Smart cameras and sensors scan the road in every direction to watch for cars, bikes, and crossing people.

q: Why is a heavy bowling ball harder to stop than a light plastic ball?
a: Bowling balls create zero friction on wood
Plastic sticks to your hands more easily
Heavier moving objects need more force to stop
Light balls have far more momentum
e: That heavy bowling ball packs lots of momentum, so stopping it takes real muscle!

q: What pushes the pistons up and down inside a gasoline car engine?
a: Magnets pushing against the car hood
Wind blowing through the front grill
e: Spark plugs ignite tiny sprays of gasoline, creating little bursts of pressure that pump the pistons!

q: Why do astronauts often wear eye masks when they go to sleep on the space station?
a: The cabin lights can never be shut off
To protect their eyes from dust
Space makes their eyes very dry
The Sun rises sixteen times every day
e: Orbiting Earth super fast brings a new sunrise every ninety minutes, making sleep tricky without a mask!

q: What specifically causes starlight to bend back and forth as it travels down to us?
a: Layers of warm and cool air moving
e: Warm and cool air constantly mix together, bending starlight back and forth like a little dance.

q: What makes a yo-yo grab the string and climb back up to your hand?
e: A little tug creates friction, catching the string so the spinning yo-yo rolls right back home!

q: Why do astronauts avoid eating crumbly food like crackers and bread in space?
a: Bread turns poisonous in zero gravity
Floating crumbs can get into eyes and machines
Crumbs smell bad inside the spacecraft
Space food must always be completely frozen
e: Floating crumbs can drift into sensitive computers or an astronaut's eyes, causing all sorts of trouble.

q: Which moon orbiting Jupiter holds the record for being the largest moon in our solar system?
e: Ganymede is a giant icy world that is actually bigger than the planet Mercury!

q: About how old do scientists believe planet Earth is?
e: By testing very old rocks and space meteorites, scientists discovered Earth has been spinning for billions of years.

q: Why do skateboarders bend their knees when riding down a bumpy sidewalk?
a: To lower balance and absorb bumps
e: Bent knees act like built-in shock absorbers, keeping your body steady over every sudden bump.

q: What happens to the pitch when a guitarist presses a string against a fretboard?
e: Pressing the string makes the vibrating part shorter, which speeds up the wiggles for higher notes.

q: What stays behind when ocean water evaporates in shallow pools under the sun?
e: Only pure water floats up into the sky, leaving sparkly salt crystals resting on the ground!

q: When you touch an ice cube, in which direction does heat naturally travel?
a: From the ice into your hand
From your warm hand into the ice
e: Heat always travels on a one-way trip from warmer spots to cooler ones!

q: UV radiation is most damaging to which human organ?
e: Our skin bravely wraps our whole body on the outside, so it catches all the sunburn from UV rays.

q: Why do astronaut helmets have a thin shiny layer of real gold on their visors?
a: To protect their eyes from dangerous solar radiation
To make the helmet look fancy for photos
To help them see in pitch-black shadows
To keep the glass from cracking when bumped
e: Gold acts like giant sunglasses, reflecting blazing sunlight to keep astronaut eyes safe and sound!

q: Where does your shadow point as the Sun sets in the west?
e: With the Sun sinking in the west, your shadow stretches out toward the east.

q: Why does a lump of soft clay go splat instead of bouncing like rubber?
a: Clay is too cold to bounce
Rubber balls do not feel gravity
Clay stays squished instead of springing back
Clay has too much trapped air inside
e: Rubber snaps right back into shape, but squishy clay just stays stuck flat.

q: Which ancient country first invented the magnetic compass to help people find their way?
e: Inventors in ancient China discovered how magnetic stones point North thousands of years ago.

q: Where is extra electricity from daytime solar panels usually stored for nighttime use?
e: Big rechargeable batteries save up that daytime sunshine to keep your lights glowing tonight!

q: Why do gymnasts dust chalk on their hands before swinging on the bars?
a: To increase friction for a better grip
To make their fingers weigh less
e: Dry chalk absorbs sweat and boosts friction, helping athletes hold on tight without slipping.

q: In which American state did the Wright brothers make their historic first powered flight?
e: Kitty Hawk in North Carolina had steady ocean winds and soft sandy dunes for a gentle landing.

q: What is the dark stripe on the back of many gift cards and hotel keys made of?
a: Tiny magnetic particles that store secret data
e: Millions of microscopic magnetic specks are arranged like a code to unlock doors or buy treats.

q: Why does a fresh unpeeled orange float, while a peeled orange sinks?
a: The peel repels water with juice
Peeling the fruit makes it heavier
The orange peel has tiny air pockets
e: That bumpy orange skin is packed with tiny air bubbles that work just like a mini life jacket!

q: Which American car maker used moving assembly lines to build cars much faster in 1913?
e: Henry Ford moved cars along a track so workers could build them quickly and affordably.

q: Where does the spongy cork used in bulletin boards and bottle stoppers come from?
e: Cork oak trees grow a thick, squishy layer of bark that can be peeled off without harming the tree.

q: How does sweat cool your body down after running around outside?
a: Sweat evaporates and carries heat away
e: As sweat floats off your skin into the air, it takes your extra heat along for the ride!

q: What bumps together inside storm clouds to make electricity build up?
e: Swirling ice bits bump into each other like socks on a rug, making lots of static electricity!

q: Why can you not hear a clear echo inside a small bathroom?
a: Sound bounces back too fast to notice
Bathroom tiles swallow all sound waves
Soap bubbles in the air block sound
e: The bounce happens so quickly that your brain hears both sounds as just one.

q: Which three metals are naturally attracted to everyday magnets?
e: These three metal cousins share a special secret: their tiny atoms line up to love magnets!

q: What is the name of the brightest true star seen in Earth's night sky?
e: Sirius, also called the Dog Star, sparkles with incredible brightness on crisp winter nights.

q: What movement of the Earth creates our daily pattern of day and night?
e: Earth spins like a top, taking turns facing toward and away from sunlight.

q: What water elevator system lifts or lowers boats between different water levels?
e: Canal locks fill or drain with water to gently float ships up or down steep hills.

q: What part of a clarinet vibrates when a musician blows air into it?
e: That tiny slice of cane wood flutters like a butterfly wing, sending lively buzzes straight through the clarinet!

q: In which unusual way does Venus rotate compared to most other planets?
a: It spins upside down every hour
It spins end-over-end like a wheel
e: While Earth spins to the east, Venus playfully twirls backwards in the opposite direction.

q: What is the location of the moon at the new moon stage?
a: Between the earth and the sun
On the opposite side of the earth from the sun
On the opposite side of the sun from the earth
To the side of a line between the earth and the sun
e: During a new moon, the moon tiptoes right between Earth and the sun, turning its bright, shiny face away to play hide-and-seek.

q: A total solar eclipse can occur only during what phase of the moon?
e: The moon must step right between Earth and the sun, hiding its bright face as a shadowy new moon.

q: Approximately what percentage of water on Earth is fresh water?
e: Earth is a giant blue puddle, but only three percent is sweet fresh water we can actually drink.

q: A lunar eclipse can occur only during what phase of the moon?
e: Earth hides the sun's light by stepping right between them, casting its cozy shadow only when the moon is completely full.
